title: Logistics & Supply Chain
tagline: How goods move through Dubai: Jebel Ali, customs, Incoterms, warehousing, inventory maths and last-mile delivery.

superpower.name: Supply Chain Pro
superpower.description: Moves goods smart: lower costs for your ventures and more from logistics jobs.

syllabus: Week 1: Dubai's trade hub: ports, airports and free zones
Week 4: Last-mile delivery and e-commerce logistics

weeks.title: Dubai's Trade Hub
weeks.objective: Understand why so much world trade flows through Dubai.

slides.title: Ports, Airports and Free Zones
slides.body: Dubai sits between Asia, Europe and Africa and has built logistics infrastructure to match. Jebel Ali Port is the largest port in the Middle East, next to the JAFZA free zone; Al Maktoum International (DWC) and DXB handle air cargo.
bullets: Jebel Ali Port: one of the world's busiest container ports
JAFZA: a free zone where companies can import, store and re-export
Sea-air: goods arrive by ship and leave by air within hours
Re-export: much of Dubai's trade is goods passing through to other markets
slides.takeaway: Dubai's edge is location plus connected sea, air and free zones.

slides.title: The Supply Chain
slides.body: A supply chain is every step from raw material to the customer: plan, source, make, deliver and return. Logistics is the physical part: moving and storing goods.
bullets: Upstream: suppliers and manufacturers
Midstream: warehouses and distribution centres
Downstream: retailers and customers
Reverse logistics: returns and recycling
slides.takeaway: A chain is only as fast as its slowest link.

weeks.title: Shipping Terms and Customs
weeks.objective: Use Incoterms correctly and clear goods through customs.

slides.title: Incoterms 2020
slides.body: Incoterms are international rules that say who pays for transport, insurance and risk at each step. Getting them wrong causes surprise bills.
bullets: EXW (Ex Works): the buyer does almost everything from the seller's door
FOB (Free On Board, sea): the seller loads it onto the ship; risk passes then
CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight, sea): the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port
DAP: delivered to a place, buyer pays import duty
DDP: the seller delivers with duty paid
slides.takeaway: Agree the Incoterm before the price: it decides who pays for what.

slides.title: Customs and Duty
slides.body: Goods entering the UAE mainland are cleared by customs (Dubai Customs in Dubai) using HS codes. Most goods pay the GCC common duty of 5% of the CIF value, with exemptions and higher rates for some products.
bullets: HS code: the international code that classifies each product
Documents: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, certificate of origin
Standard duty: 5% of CIF value for most goods
VAT at 5% is also due on imports
slides.example:
Importing furniture with a CIF value of AED 40,000:
Customs duty: 5% × 40,000 = AED 2,000
Import VAT: 5% × (40,000 + 2,000) = AED 2,100
Total at the border: AED 4,100
slides.takeaway: Correct HS codes and documents mean fast clearance and no fines.

weeks.title: Warehousing and Inventory
weeks.objective: Store goods efficiently and order the right amount at the right time.

slides.title: Warehouse Operations
slides.body: A warehouse is a factory for orders: receive, put away, store, pick, pack and ship. Speed and accuracy both matter.
bullets: FIFO (first in, first out) for most goods; FEFO (first expiry, first out) for food and medicine
ABC analysis: A items (high value) get the most attention
Cold chain: medicines often 2 to 8°C, frozen food −18°C
A warehouse management system (WMS) tracks every location
slides.takeaway: The right item in the right place, found in seconds.

slides.title: Inventory Maths
slides.body: Too much stock ties up cash; too little loses sales. Two formulas help balance it.
bullets: Reorder point = daily demand × lead time + safety stock
Economic order quantity (EOQ) = √(2 × annual demand × order cost ÷ holding cost per unit)
Safety stock covers surprises in demand or delays
Stock turnover = cost of sales ÷ average stock
slides.example:
A shop sells 40 units a day; the supplier takes 7 days; safety stock is 60.
Reorder point: 40 × 7 + 60 = 340 units.
Annual demand 12,000, order cost AED 100, holding cost AED 4 per unit a year:
EOQ = √(2 × 12,000 × 100 ÷ 4) = √600,000 ≈ 775 units per order
slides.takeaway: Order by maths, not by feeling.

weeks.title: Last-Mile and E-Commerce Logistics
weeks.objective: Deliver fast, cheaply and reliably to customers' doors.

slides.title: The Last Mile
slides.body: The last mile, from the local hub to the customer, is often the most expensive part of delivery. In Dubai, customers expect same-day or next-day delivery.
bullets: Route planning to cut kilometres and fuel
Delivery slots and live tracking reduce failed deliveries
Cash on delivery is still common in the region and adds risk
Lockers and pick-up points cut failed attempts
slides.takeaway: Failed deliveries are the hidden cost: confirm, track, deliver once.

slides.title: Measuring Performance
slides.body: Logistics teams track a few numbers to keep improving.
bullets: On-time delivery %
First-attempt delivery success %
Cost per delivery
Return rate and reasons
slides.example:
A courier made 1,200 delivery attempts this week and 1,050 succeeded first time.
First-attempt success: 1,050 ÷ 1,200 = 87.5%
If each failed attempt costs AED 12 to redo: 150 × 12 = AED 1,800 a week lost.
slides.takeaway: Measure every week; fix the biggest leak first.
